source_figures.caption: Experimental setup. (A) We exposed epithelial cells to frictional shear stress relevant to airway reopening in our setup. (B) A single bubble is propagated over cell monolayer by filling the chamber and then retracting fluid over the cells. (C) The parallel plate flow chamber is composed of an upper cover slip, a cell-seeded lower coverslip, and a membrane sandwiched between two coverslips. (D) A propagating bubble is seen. (E) Fluorescent live/dead stain method is used to assess viability. Here, green represents calcein-stained live cells, and red are ethidium-stained dead cells.

chapters.title: An injured cell in an idealized airway
chapters.speech: When an air liquid boundary moves across epithelial cells, mechanical forces can cause injury. This question motivated a controlled laboratory model, not a trial in patients.
chapters.source: Methods and Protocols 2020 3(4):65, introduction and setup.

chapters.title: The original chamber
chapters.speech: The published apparatus drives fluid over cells through a parallel plate flow chamber. Its components define the model, including the cover slips and the narrow channel.
chapters.source: 2020 methods article Figure 1, original experimental apparatus.

chapters.title: One moving interface
chapters.speech: A bubble advances across the monolayer, exposing cells to forces near the moving interface. Our animation explains the geometry without inventing numerical stress measurements.
chapters.source: Figure 1A conceptual mechanics; no quantitative stress field simulated.

chapters.title: Make the geometry repeatable
chapters.speech: The cell bearing cover slip sits beneath a gasket and a second cover slip. Repeating that arrangement helps isolate exposure while limiting what the apparatus can represent.

chapters.title: Injury becomes visible
chapters.speech: In the original L2 cell experiment, controls showed almost no cell death. The bubble exposed group averaged around fifty three percent dead cells, across seven experimental repetitions.
chapters.source: 2020 methods paper, Expected Results, Figure 5 A–C; control 0–0.2% and bubble ~53%, seven repetitions.

chapters.title: Actin provides another view
chapters.speech: The actin images reveal a subtler picture. There was no significant overall change in cytoskeletal structure after one bubble, although the authors observed slight differences in filament orientation.
chapters.source: Figure 6 and published Effects on Cytoskeletal Structure; orientation difference only, no significant structure difference.

chapters.title: What the images establish
chapters.speech: A mechanical insult in a simplified system can change cell viability and organization. It does not by itself tell us how a patient's entire respiratory tract will respond.
chapters.source: Source paper Results and Discussion; in-vitro model limitations.

chapters.title: A model, not a lung
chapters.speech: The chamber makes a hidden physical event experimentally accessible. Its strength is repeatability; its limit is the distance between a cell monolayer and the living lung.
chapters.source: Experimental model scope; no clinical extrapolation.
